batchSummary: Reviewed all 37 images, V115–V151. This draft batch develops channel applications, room/people/red guardrails, human-rendering studies, character references and production checklists. Strong recurring cues are warm architectural space, product-first framing, tactile detail and supported everyday activity. Important unresolved issues include contradictory red examples, fashion-oriented character poses, incomplete channel demonstrations and an inconsistent scorecard. All rules and ‘locked’ characters remain draft proposals—not evidence of adoption, product efficacy or quality approval.

relationships.finding: The main guide template uses red selectively, while the character appendix uses a different graphic language.
relationships.interpretation: Cream pages repeat a red wordmark, black/red serif headlines and small metadata. The appendix switches to black dividers, handwritten boards, photo grids and unbranded studio triptychs. These reference-board treatments should not be mistaken for a resolved public-facing Duroflex identity system.

relationships.finding: Architectural calm is most convincingly demonstrated through openings, floor area and layered low-contrast surfaces.
relationships.interpretation: Screen-like glazing or garden openings provide directional light; rugs and low platforms anchor products; olive, cream and wood-toned layers avoid visual flatness. Borrow those spatial relationships, adapting the room to the exact SKU rather than recolouring the product or adding artificial contrast patches.

relationships.finding: Repeated assets demonstrate a proposed reusable image library, not separate channel executions.
relationships.interpretation: The frontal blue-edged mattress, isolated teal loveseat and red-accented bedrooms recur across PDP, performance and launch propositions. This supports reusable room, icon and detail coverage, but does not demonstrate working interfaces, CTA placement, proof modules or completed campaign adaptations.

relationships.finding: The role of the crowded red room becomes explicit only in the guardrails sequence.
relationships.interpretation: Earlier application collages mix the saturated room with quieter examples without clear labels. Later pages consistently place it under DON’T. Its ornate styling, presentation gestures and red saturation should therefore be read as a negative comparator, not spatial inspiration to reproduce.

relationships.finding: The proposed red principle is clearer than its affirmative examples.
relationships.interpretation: The text advocates controlled punctuation, yet positive-looking examples combine red bedding, cushions, benches, mugs, books or clothing. Graphic red, authentic product details and optional room accents need separate definitions before production; the examples do not override exact-SKU preservation.

relationships.finding: Domestic activity references and character-presentation references serve different purposes.
relationships.interpretation: Reading, pillow contact and supported reclining show how people might inhabit products. Casting boards prioritise direct gaze, garment display, athletic settings or posed stance. Borrow appearance continuity and surface detail from the latter, but re-stage activity rather than transferring fashion poses directly into inhabited heroes.

relationships.finding: The human-rendering studies provide a coherent contact-and-surface checklist.
relationships.interpretation: Across these pages, pores through highlights, hair density, non-identical fingers, pressure, seams and force-related folds recur. Applied together, these checks can support believable product/person interaction. Added skin texture alone cannot repair unsupported weight, incorrect anatomy or inconsistent light.

relationships.finding: Scenic recliner imagery sits uneasily beside the more credible domestic bedroom language.
relationships.interpretation: The flowering arch and distant scenic view offer a more escapist setting than garden-connected, warm modern bedrooms. Borrow the recliner’s clear silhouette if useful, but adapt the setting toward ordinary home restoration rather than importing resort-style wellness or copying a regional aesthetic.

relationships.finding: Visual proof and product efficacy remain distinct throughout the batch.
relationships.interpretation: Clean product views and simplified technical communication align with the supplied preference for thoughtful innovation and no overpromising. Neither attractive rooms, exposed layers nor relaxed people establish stress-release, pain-relief or other exact-product outcomes.

relationships.finding: Movement is proposed through poses and sequences, but no motion execution is available.
relationships.interpretation: Stretching, hair movement and walking sequences suggest changes in body state. They cannot establish transition speed, continuity, believable inertia or the absence of frantic editing. Motion evaluation requires the actual clips.

relationships.finding: The six-item delivery list can extend the earlier four-class shoot system, but its mapping is unstated.
relationships.interpretation: World, Inhabited Hero and Icon have close equivalents; Details could supply Intelligence assets, while Performance and Sale appear to be channel derivatives. Clarifying that mapping would prevent duplicate deliverables and distinguish source photography from graphic adaptations.

contradictions: V128 prohibits red bedding and props while its DO image includes a red bed runner, cushion and bench. V124 additionally presents red mugs, a book and burgundy clothing within its positive human board.

V126’s activity-led, non-performing proposition contrasts with the fashion poses in V144–V147. These may be useful casting studies, but their inclusion does not resolve suitability for consumer-facing inhabited scenes.

V127 emphasises quiet homewear and rejects branded athleisure and synthetic shine; V142 explicitly proposes athleisure, while V143 depicts lustrous pyjamas. This requires a styling clarification, not an inference that the garments are branded or made from synthetic fibres.
V151 states a 100-point score but lists only eight 10-point criteria. Its pass/refine thresholds cannot be used consistently without correcting the scoring structure.
V130 reintroduces PART V and footer page 17 inside the surrounding PART VIII sequence; V136 then says ‘Locked Characters’. This editorial assembly does not establish formal locking or approval.
V149’s suggestion to reduce distracting labels is too broad for exact-product imagery: authentic product branding must remain preserved under the client scene policy.
gaps: Exact-SKU source assets, verified construction details, colour/fabric references and approved branding files are not supplied here. Rendered deck typography may also contain font substitutions.

V118 does not show a storefront; V119 does not show a complete retail layout; V116–V121 do not demonstrate usable PDP, marketplace or advertising interfaces. No current-site comparison can be established from these draft collages.
V129 lacks a positive science example. Technical details and any efficacy language need product-specific substantiation beyond the May 2025 positioning.
Reference authenticity, actual material composition, dimensions, camera/film provenance and printed character identities remain unverified. ‘Locked’ does not establish adoption or quality approval.
Only stills are available. Motion pacing, body transitions, mechanism movement and temporal consistency remain unreviewed.

The prompt toolkit omits operational requirements for exact-product preservation, architectural negative space, coherent shadows/occlusion/contact and supported anatomy; these need explicit production controls.
The scorecard needs its missing 20 points or a revised denominator, and the four-class/six-deliverable asset taxonomy needs reconciliation before production use.
Many embedded contact-sheet captions and product labels are too small for dependable detailed reading; their presence does not verify named products, offers or claims.
